rows.speaker: the majority
rows.claim: The majority holds that Luqmān was a sage rather than a prophet.
rows.anchor: the majority is that he was not a prophet. He was, in fact, a sage

rows.speaker: Some historians
rows.claim: Some historians regard Luqmān as a king.
rows.anchor: Some historians regard him to be a king.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author thinks Luqmān was a chief; jāhiliyyah poetry portrays him as the patriarchal head of his Yemeni tribe.
rows.anchor: The way the jāhiliyyah poets have mentioned him shows that he was the patriarchal head of his tribe in Yemen.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author infers that Luqmān gave this counsel when his son was being crowned the next tribal chief.
rows.anchor: they were imparted to him at the time when he was being crowned as the next tribal chief.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude to God is wisdom’s first consequence and its clearest sign; it grounds all duties to God and other people.
rows.anchor: The first consequence of wisdom is being grateful to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that gratitude benefits the grateful person is an apt insertion, clarifying that God commands it for people’s benefit.
rows.anchor: They form an appropriate on the spot insertion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thankfulness benefits its practitioner: God’s favors increase for the grateful person in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: He who remains thankful to God will see that God’s favours on Him will increase in this world and the next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is self-sufficient and unaffected by human gratitude or ingratitude; as Ḥamīd, He possesses personal, lofty attributes no creature can change.
rows.anchor: Neither is the gratitude of a person beneficial to Him nor is someone’s ingratitude harmful to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God continues to give favors and sustenance whether people value them or not; the author connects this attribute to 31:26.
rows.anchor: God’s favours on Him will increase in this world and the next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The essence of gratitude is avoiding polytheism: since God grants all favors, thanks to others are subordinate to thanks to Him.
rows.anchor: similarly the true essence of gratitude is abstinence from polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Associating others with God usurps His greatest right and is therefore the greatest injustice.
rows.anchor: he is guilty of usurping the greatest of rights – and there is nothing more unjust than this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān delivered this counsel deliberately and elaborately on a specific occasion, stressing that his son should adhere to it.
rows.anchor: they were said on a specific occasion in an elaborate way as advice to his son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān directs its audience to compare what a wise father teaches his son with how they themselves treat their children.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to direct the attention of the addressees of the Qur’ān what a wise father teaches his son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God inserts the parent verses into Luqmān’s counsel: Luqmān modestly omits his own parental right, then turns to Judgment Day, so God supplies the missing guidance.
rows.anchor: These two verses are insertions from God within the verses of counsel from Luqmān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parents have the greatest human right after God; all prophets and divine books teach kindness to parents after fulfilling God’s right.
rows.anchor: all prophets and books of God have unanimously taught people that after the right of God, it is essential to treat parents with kindness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After God, parents have the greatest right because they bring a person into existence and nourish them.
rows.anchor: as far as gratitude and service are concerned, the children are directed to do so in the case of both the father and the mother.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parental right is gratitude and service, not worship.
rows.anchor: as far as gratitude and service are concerned, the children are directed to do so in the case of both the father and the mother.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True gratitude requires fulfilling promises; verbal thanks without fulfillment are baseless.
rows.anchor: Here all the three phases of pregnancy, birth and suckling are referred to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Children must refuse parental demands to commit polytheism, which has no proof or supporting argument; every polytheist nevertheless believes in God.
rows.anchor: besides not obeying their parents in matters of polytheism they at all cost must follow the way of those who are tuned to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even when parents are disbelievers, children must treat them kindly, meet their needs where possible, and pray for their guidance; Abraham prayed for his father until God stopped him.
rows.anchor: if the children fully recognized the right of God together with the right of their parents and adhered to it in a steadfast way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completely severing ties with disbelieving parents is allowed only when the Muslim community collectively disavows them and their nation.
rows.anchor: if some parents by misusing the right granted to them by God force their children to abandon the path of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names the mother’s pregnancy, birth, and suckling, but no paternal labor, so the mother has a greater right than the father.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this that a mother has a greater right on her children than a father.

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says the mother’s right is three times the father’s; the author says this narrative is based on this verse.
rows.anchor: the narrative of the Prophet (sws) is based which says that the right of the mother is thrice that of a father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return to God warns that people will answer for neglecting gratitude to God and fulfilling parents’ rights.
rows.anchor: everyone should bear in mind that at last finally everyone has to turn to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Children must follow those devoted to God, not even parents who have left His path; 29:12 quotes parents inviting their dependents to follow their way, which the author rejects.
rows.anchor: not permissible to follow anyone who invites people to a path which is against the path of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final warning and assurance address both parents and children: parents who divert children from God face punishment, while steadfast children are rewarded.
rows.anchor: one day every person will return to God, and he will be shown by God all the deeds he had done.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After God’s inserted parent guidance, Luqmān resumes his counsel: monotheism comes first, followed by the hereafter as the second basic belief.
rows.anchor: After the intervening verses from God, the counsel of Luqmān resumes from here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every good or evil deed, however tiny and wherever hidden, will be brought forth on Judgment Day because God is discerning and all-knowing.
rows.anchor: God will it bring forth on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ignorance of God’s attributes leads nations into errors about monotheism and the hereafter; Luqmān corrects his son’s understanding of both.
rows.anchor: It is because of a lack of knowledge about the attributes of God because of which nations have been misled about monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “innaha” is ṣamīr al-sha’n, used for something mentally present to the speaker.
rows.anchor: is the pronoun of shā’n. In such situations, a speaker uses a pronoun for a thing in his mind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun’s referent is the knowledge of a mustard-seed-sized deed, and its feminine form agrees with habba (seed).
rows.anchor: Here this is antecedent is “knowledge of the size of the mustard seed.” It is in deference to ٍۃَّبَح that the feminine pronoun is used.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says ṣakhrah need not mean a stone; it can mean a mountain and its passes, which fits Arabic usage, and he translates accordingly.
rows.anchor: It can also refer to a mountain and its passes and this would be in conformity with linguistic principles of Arabic.

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī cites a group that interprets ṣakhrah as a mountain or its passes.
rows.anchor: Ṭabarī has also cited that one group of people interpret this word in this meaning.
